query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Premelting and melting of 5–20 nm Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy (HEA) nanoparticles are governed by Cu- and Ni-rich surface segregation that produces a Cu–Ni–enriched quasi-liquid skin; this low-melting surface layer nucleates melting heterogeneously, yielding a two-step transition (surface premelting at T₁ followed by core melting at T₂ ≈ T₁+100–200 K).
generation.material_initial_state: Random, single-phase fcc solid-solution Fe20Ni20Cr20Co20Cu20 nanoparticles (5–20 nm diameter) produced by rapid quench from the melt; chemically homogeneous in the as-synthesised state.
generation.intervention: Controlled in-situ heating (1–10 K s⁻¹) under high vacuum in a transmission-electron microscope (TEM) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) mapping.
generation.conditions: Pressure ≤10⁻⁶ Torr; temperature ramp 300 K → 1500 K; no reactive gas present.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a Cu–Ni-rich, ∼1 nm-thick quasi-liquid surface layer that wets the particle and lowers the local melting point.
generation.mechanism: Elements with the lowest surface energies (Cu, Ni) diffuse to the surface upon heating. Size mismatch and positive mixing enthalpy with the remaining elements destabilise the segregated layer, which becomes disordered and partially liquid at T₁ well below the bulk size-corrected melting point. This liquid skin seeds full melting when its thickness reaches a critical fraction of the radius.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to size-matched Cu-free Fe–Ni–Cr–Co nanoparticles, the Cu-containing HEA will: (a) display an earlier, distinct heat-capacity shoulder or DSC peak at T₁ ≈ (bulk alloy T_m – 250 ± 50 K); (b) show Cu (and Ni) enrichment at the surface (≥2× average composition) before the onset of the main melting peak; (c) melt completely only after an additional ΔT ≈ 100–200 K. The Cu-free baseline will show a single sharp melting event with no prior surface premelting signature.
generation.baseline: Compositionally similar Fe–Ni–Cr–Co nanoparticles of identical size distribution prepared and heated identically.
generation.boundary: Applicable for equiatomic (±5 at%) Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles 5–20 nm in vacuum or inert gas; breaks down for particles >30 nm (bulk-like behaviour) or under oxidising atmospheres that suppress segregation.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of ΔT and precise Cu surface enrichment factor may vary with particle size and heating rate; Cu diffusion kinetics at the smallest sizes are not well constrained.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform identical in-situ TEM heating on (i) Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu and (ii) Fe–Ni–Cr–Co nanoparticles (5–20 nm). Record high-resolution videos while continuously mapping surface composition with EDS/EELS and acquire simultaneous nanocalorimetry/DSC signals.
measurements: Onset temperature of first calorimetric event (T₁)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if Cu-containing particles do NOT exhibit (1) measurable Cu/Ni surface enrichment prior to melting, OR (2) a separate, earlier calorimetric/structural premelting transition relative to the Cu-free baseline. Observation of uniform composition with a single melting event at the same temperature as the baseline invalidates the proposed mechanism.
